utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-98-34-T, the Prosecutor versus Naletilic and Martinovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Naletilic? THE ACCUSED NALETILIC: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: How are you feeling this morning? THE ACCUSED NALETILIC: [Interpretation] Tomorrow, I should be examined at 2.00. They should take an image here behind. I don't know how it is called.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Did you see the physicians yesterday afternoon? THE ACCUSED NALETILIC: [Interpretation] Yes. No, actually, I saw the physician's assistant. She said that that feeling that I had was not good and that tomorrow they will attempt to have an appointment to have a scan made. The feeling is the same here. There is no pain in my heart area, but I have no strength here. I have no -- I had problem buttoning my jacket five days ago. That was all right. I have a feeling that it has something to do with my heart. There may be clogging of some kind. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We wish you a speedy recovery. If there is any problem with your health, please do not hesitate to let us know. THE ACCUSED NALETILIC: [Interpretation] Well, right now I feel all right, as far as my heart is concerned. It's almost a miracle. But it's all right. That is the condition. I will be examined tomorrow. Right now I can take these -- the rigour of the hearing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Please sit down, please. Yes, Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. I just wanted to say, and I assume the Chamber would want to hear concerning Mr. Naletilic this morning before the witness came in. I also felt the need to respond very briefly to a couple of things and make one clarification of the schedule. Mr. President, you indicated yesterday afternoon that perhaps this current witness, Mr. Smajkic, might have been called earlier in the case. I think just so it's clear, the record should indicate he was in fact called earlier in the case. He was here in the second week of trial. Because at the Registry's request - and I'm not talking about the registry in the courtroom - but because of the Registry's request that Mr. Mrachacz be taken out of turn, the schedule was -- there were problems in the schedule. Mr. Smajkic was here and sat here in The Hague for one week, waiting to testify. We could not get to him. He had to go back to Bosnia, so this is his second time here. So we did attempt to call him at an earlier time. Having said that, Your Honour, I do want to indicate I don't want to encourage any thinking, of course, that we are only calling all of our most important witnesses at the beginning of the case. I can assure you that we believe, of course, that all of our witnesses are important, or we wouldn't call them at all, and we do expect some important witnesses to be called at the very end of the case. So we are trying to present the case to you, perfectly or imperfectly - the latter, I'm sure - as efficiently and effectively as we can. I can assure the Chamber that every effort is being made to do that. We will stumble and fall sometimes, but we are trying to make our best efforts to do that. In that regard, I also need to announce that because, again, of the schedule problem yesterday afternoon, one of our witnesses has been cancelled and is not in The Hague and will be skipping the witness who will be listed -- Jeremy Bowen, who will be listed after this witness. I'm not going to announce the next witness name because we are in open session, but everyone who has the schedule will be able to see that the witness who follows Mr. Bowen will be the next witness following Mr. Smajkic. We will be skipping Mr. Bowen, and here, again, he will have to be worked into the schedule at some future time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you ready for your witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I would just like to use the opportunity before the witness comes back. I have a request for the Trial Chamber and also for our learned friends. No one could foresee the incidents of yesterday, and I believe that health concerns are something that we should all feel the same about. But the Defence finds itself in a difficult position simply because the witnesses are testifying out of turn. If we have a witness that the Defence is not aware of the changes, we will have problems in cross-examination. And I would just like to ask for as much notice as is possible in calling of witnesses so that we can prepare properly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, what happened yesterday is quite extraordinary. I hope you can understand the difficulties from the other side for rescheduling of the witness. Yes, could we have the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Please remember that you are still under the solemn declaration. Yes, Mr. Scott. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Smajkic, just to set the scene a bit since yesterday midday, you had told us that you had approached the Catholic bishop in Mostar to go with you -- to accompany you to a military position in your clerical clothing and destroy -- take down sandbags as a symbolic act against the war, for peace. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And unfortunately, you did not receive a favourable response from anyone on the Croat side; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to take you to the day of the 9th of May, 1993. And I would like to start, please -- can you just give us - being mindful of the desire to be somewhat brief - would you just give us your account of what happened, what you saw and heard and what happened to you on the 9th of May, 1993.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On 9th of May, 1993, in the early morning hours, I could hear heavy artillery fire and also firing from all kinds of other weapons. And so there was thunderous fire all around at the same time. Because I live near the line of separation, the present-day line of separation, near my house a river of people passed by, men, women, children, in their pyjamas, and they were moving in a direction of the eastern part of town. The fire was intense. People's hearts were freezing with the apprehension of what may happen. It was truly like hell.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Where were you at this time?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was at my home.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Where did you live in Mostar at that time?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is exactly on the Bulevar. This is the current line of separation in the city. However, I worked -- that is, my office was far into the western section of town. But that night, I was at home.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: When you say that you saw a river of people passing by, moving in the direction of the eastern part of town, can you give us a bit more of an idea of how many -- what did this river consist of? Approximately how many people did you see moving toward the east part of town?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was accompanied by shrieks and screams and fire. There was an underpass under the main road where people were being directed by fire, literally by bullets, into this canal where the people were supposed to pass towards -- in the eastern section of town. In other words, this fire was directed, and the people were almost stampeded towards the eastern section of town by my house.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Meek?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Your Honours, I must object. The answer is non-responsive. The question was very simple. Could he answer how many he saw. We have gone into six or seven lines, and he is still describing the scene, not giving the answer to the question, which is the number of people he observed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: In this point, I agree with you, but the witness describes a very vivid picture of what happened that morning. We feel very interested in hearing this witness on this situation. But the question is really how many people.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Smajkic, let me go back, please, to that part of my question, excepting everything else you have said. Can you give us an idea of how many people did you see moving in the direction of the eastern part of town, as you've described it? Not in a precise number, but 10, 15, 50, 100, thousands?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not possible to say that precisely because this was a column of people, people - men, women, children - pyjamas, who were roused from their beds and left their homes in order to save their lives. There must have been at least a hundred. I saw them. I saw them. They passed by my house. Basically they just brushed against a wall of my house. I didn't count them. In addition, the fire was continuous. You could only peek out, because you ran a risk of being hit by a bullet yourself.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you know at that time or did you come to know that in addition to the people that you saw moving in the direction of the east part of the city, that other Bosniaks were being taken to other places?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I learned from some of these people whom I recognised, who dropped in to take a drink of water, that some people were being taken towards the stadium.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, did you hear about this time or did you learn about that time that a particular Muslim church official, an imam, I believe you described yesterday, that an imam was killed on the 9th or 10th of May?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That was not at that time. That was the next day. That was the next day. Because I was unable to move about. I waited for the nightfall to cross the Neretva River, because I live on the right bank on the other side of Neretva, so I needed to wait for the nightfall to cross over and make inquiries stealthily so that I could be safe.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me reverse the order, then, of my questions. Let's finish with what you just began telling us and then go back to the question about the imam. What happened on the 9th in terms of this: Did you stay in your house or did you at some point move to another location?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stayed that night, stayed on late. Later on, they looked for me. They wondered whether I had been captured by the HVO. I simply could not budge, I could not step out, because of all the fire that was raging. If I can be -- if I can describe it graphically, one of my neighbours in the house next to me -- let me say that this line, the line of separation, was already being established there. The ABiH was -- had already set up positions there, and there was no movement forward there. And one of the neighbours took something to -- some food to those who had been fortifying these positions there at that time, and he was wounded. He had some food in his hand. He was only going to cross the street, and he was unable to make it across.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Please tell us what happened to you and how you then moved to wherever it is that you went after leaving your house?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our headquarters, our command, the ABiH command, was inquiring whether I was alive or not, because rumours were spreading then. One of the imams who had been captured and -- by the HVO, and I lived nearby, so they wanted me to come and confirm that. They wanted me to simply appear there, because we needed -- they needed to put together some announcement, public announcement. That night, when I finally made it there, I learned about this case of my colleague who lived deeper into their territory. They captured him, and then that same day they executed him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. And I'm going back to my question now. Where did you go after leaving your house on the Bulevar? How did you get there?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went to the ABiH command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you stay there continuously, then, throughout the siege, or where did you live after this?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I went there because Mr. Pasalic, Mr. Arif Pasalic, the commander of our corps, had gone several days before to negotiate a Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. cease-fire with the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm going to cut you off. We do have to move forward. Please listen to my question. I must say you're not answering my question at this point. You lived -- your house was on the Bulevar?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You left your house sometime, if I understand you correctly - if I'm wrong, please correct me - sometime on the evening of the 9th. You were able to move to the -- an ABiH headquarters or field base to assist in some way. Now, after that happened, did you return to your house on the Bulevar and did you live there, then, throughout the siege of East Mostar, or did you go some place else? That's my question.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went back to my house.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And then how long did you continue to live at your house?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was there for several days. I had an elderly father and my family, and the line of separation was being fortified there, so I went to Donja Mahala, which is about 300 metres down towards the Hum hill.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Were you stopped by anyone on your way to this new location in Donja Mahala?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By the time I was -- it was discovered that I was there, the line had been set up there, so I found myself sort of like in neutral, no man's land. But later on, the forces of ABiH led me out late at night. It was almost the morning when they led me out and took me to the headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Now, let's go back to the imam. Was there an imam named Salem Mezit who you learned was killed on around the 9th or 10th of May, 1993?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was the imam that we were referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can you just tell the Chamber what happened to this Imam Mezit?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was simply executed in front of his house.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And did you learn or were you told by who he was executed?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Later on, we inquired through the Red Cross. It was sometime later, we wanted to find out the truth. But the people who were moving from the west side to the east saw him being led away from his house. This is deeper into the west side from where I lived. So this mass of people, this crowd, observed that he was taken out, separated from the crowd, and immediately executed on the spot.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you describe for us, a bit more, if you can, by location or street, the approximate location where Mr. Mezit was killed.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is exactly across from the Catholic church's convent, 200 or 300 metres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is this a neighbourhood or suburb called Podhum?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, Podhum.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you ever speak with the imam's wife who may have told you more of what happened?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: She told me that several nights before, in anticipation of this attack, several -- that is, he and several men went to their relatives in the eastern section of town fearing what might happen. So that night, he went back and spent the night there. And this, I guess, is what was meant to happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me direct your attention --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If the witness could be - if he doesn't have it still - the packet of exhibits from yesterday. Mr. Usher, there's a binder of exhibits, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If you can turn to -- in fact, it will be the one that we left off from yesterday. If you can find, please -- it should be about halfway through the bundle, Exhibit P410, which is a letter from you and one other person on the 23rd of May, 1993. Do you have that?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you just tell the Chamber what that document is and how it relates to what you've just been telling us about.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This relates to the fact that from the HVO, from the person in charge of medical matters, we received information that certain persons, including Salem Mezit, the imam, were in the hospital. And we were asked to come in order to identify these persons. In fact - and this was strange - Salem Mezit was described as a member of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: To your knowledge, was that true? Was he a member of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In fact, I do know that he was not a member of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me briefly stop you for a moment. We touched on this yesterday, but you described Mr. Mezit as a imam. Was he local, like a neighbourhood or some sort of local Islamic church leader? What was his position or role?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the imam of a particular mosque in the city of Mostar, and also of a neighbourhood in Mostar, a neighbourhood which we term "Mahala" in the city. So that is his activities in the mosque, certain services including weddings, births, and other religious ceremonies.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Are you able to give us the name of the particular mosque that he was associated with?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the Dervis Pasha mosque, which is now non-existent. It was destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you know when that mosque was destroyed?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The mosque had been partially damaged during the Serbo-Chetnik aggression. It was shelled. But then it was completely destroyed when the HVO attacked.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: When you say when the HVO attacked, was it destroyed in connection with the 9th and 10th of May, 1993, or sometime after that?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, on that date.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Just so the record is clear, you are saying it was destroyed on the 9th or 10th of May?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, your letter, which is Exhibit P410, also goes on to say -- before I ask you one or two questions, just to finish --

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, may I, just in regard of this letter, before we --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: We're not finished with it. Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had asked from the Red Cross to be allowed to visit other locations because we had learned that in this campaign, several imams had been taken prisoners and that several mosques had been destroyed. So this is why we gave certain names and certain locations, in Capljina, Stolac, and the west side of the city. And you can see here that my archives in my office in the western part of town had been seized. So through the Red Cross, I asked to be allowed to take my archives and the archive of the Islamic community offices in Mostar. However, to this date, this request has not been met. And I think that -- I wanted to mention that because that is also something that is referred to in this letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Let me just ask you a final question on this letter. Were you, then, ever - at that time - given the opportunity to make the requested inquiry concerning the Imam Salem Mezit or concerning the other properties mentioned in your letter?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They never responded to this letter, nor did they send any verbal message back to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Smajkic, I'm going to ask you just a couple -- just a few questions about the time -- during the time that Mostar was under what some might describe as a siege. Was there a sniping campaign against the Muslims in the east side of Mostar and do you know, and can you tell the Chamber, based on your observations, were civilians targeted during that sniping?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Anything that could move -- to put it simply, anything that could move was a target of sniper attacks; that is to say, civilians, animals. For example, even later, in the neighbourhood in the Mahala, I saw them targeting goats, sheep, anything that could move; civilians included, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Were you ever, in fact, in close proximity to someone who was hit by sniper fire?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Very often, we would have to run across on crossroads. We had to make certain protective barriers so that we could run across the street and avoid being hit by sniper fire. On one occasion, as we were running across the street, one of the people who was with me was hit in the leg, although there was a kind of protective barrier camouflaged in a way. But he was hit, nevertheless. This did not really provide for a safe passage, and it was a pretty primitive protection. But often I was in the hospital, in the hospital where I saw civilians who were being treated. I didn't see when they were actually hit, but I would see them in hospital receiving treatment, and I heard that they were hit while crossing the street. Therefore, the municipal government that had just been established then - established from scratch, because the entire infrastructure was in the western part of town, so some kind of organisation had to be set up very fast - and these authorities --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Meek?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, I must object again to the non-responsiveness of this answer. The question again appears to be fairly simple. Yes, yes, he answered it. He gave the example. And now he's just aimlessly babbling. And I object to the way this is being answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object to the characterisation of the witness babbling. It may or may not be a longer answer than counsel would like, but it is not appropriate to refer to the witness as babbling, and I object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, we believe that the answer is just to the question, but it's just a little bit too long. And the question is very simple: Did you see someone who was hit by sniper fire? It's a very simple question. Mr. Scott, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, let me go back to that particular incident. I appreciate the information about the hospitals, and I do believe it's relevant for this Chamber to hear, but let me go back to the person that you were with at the time that you said he or she - and you haven't told us whether it was a he or she - but was hit by sniper fire. First of all, was this -- you don't have to use the person's name, if you think you would prefer not to identify him, at least in my view - counsel may have a different view - but who was this person that was with you, just by description? Was it a relative? Just a friend? Can you just tell us a bit more about the person who was struck?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is a man. My wife's uncle, as a matter of fact, to be as brief as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can you tell the Chamber, at the time that he was struck, to your knowledge -- first of all, was he -- as far as you know, was he a civilian?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A civilian invariably. Never put a uniform on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And my next question is: At the moment he was struck, was he wearing civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was wearing normal, civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let's move on. I've talked to you now about sniping, in terms of with what people might consider to be rifle fire. Was there also a campaign that involved artillery or mortar shelling of East Mostar?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All calibres were used in the shelling, incessantly, day and night, and also unselectively; that is to say, everything was being destroyed, monumental buildings of historic importance, private homes, the hospital. To put it simply, as people were being targeted, buildings and all other edifices were being fired at, shelled, from all possible weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Very briefly, can you tell the Chamber were there any civilian gatherings that you remember, either particular -- by particular incident or just the nature of the gatherings themselves, that were targeted, that were shelled, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can point out that gatherings were also targeted, any kind of gathering.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Such as?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can particularly emphasise that because of the fact that we lived in a town without any water supply. Water comes from the western part of town, and the water supply was cut off, and therefore, we used cisterns. We took water from the Neretva River, and we went into the small streets, alleys, where people waited for water to be given to them from this cistern and put into smaller vessels. When people would find out that the water cistern was coming in, a generator would be turned on so that water could actually come out of the cistern. The HVO soldiers Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. heard the engines, heard the generators, and then they would actually aim at such a group of people, at such a gathering. That happened all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Meek, I think this witness is just telling the story how those gatherings were hit by the shellings.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Your Honours, my point is simply this: That the question asked, does he know whether or not any gatherings were targeted. I think that any answer is speculation because any gathering that might have been hit could very easily have been accidental. This witness, not being from the other army, and being a civilian, would have no idea as to whether anything was targeted. For example, we know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Meek, that's a very strange objection. Very, very strange.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: It calls for speculation. What's strange, Your Honour? I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Why is it speculation?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: How would he know if any location was specifically targeted or if it was accidentally hit by an accident? For example --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: No, no. No matter whether is purposely targeted or accidentally hit, but they are hit by the shellings. That's the truth, and this witness knows those things happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, very briefly, there are at least two ways in which this is extremely relevant to the overall case and for this Chamber to know some of the things that happened in Mostar, in which these accused also carried out, as charged in the indictment, various acts: There was either indiscriminate sniping and shelling in which there was no regard who they were shooting at, which we submit is itself a war crime, indiscriminate fire. Or there was intentional targeting of civilians, which itself is a war crime. Either way a crime was committed, if we are able to prove that. That's one of the reasons this evidence is relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, I have to stop you. Here you are just to make clear what the facts are, not the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, but I do have to respond when counsel makes an objection to speculation and relevance, as to why it is in fact proper evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: This Trial Chamber has already made the rulings. You just abide by the rulings and proceed with your direct examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you -- you've used the word "cistern," which -- what do you mean by "cistern," because it seems to be a word that my past experience has not -- a word that not many of us would use? Are you talking about a cistern being a well in the ground, or what was it that was moving this water around that you were telling us about?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's like a fire-fighting vehicle actually. But it's like a water truck. It carries water. And then this water that is pumped into this truck is then distributed throughout town.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. So now when you go back to your testimony now a few minutes ago, would you pick up, then, and tell us, before the interruption, when was it that the HVO fire would start in this regard?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said quite precisely, and I want to say this clearly and unequivocally, it was not only once that this happened. Whenever these water trucks that were providing water - because there were no operating waterworks. This water truck moved through town, and it was seeking shelter behind buildings so that it would not be a target for the HVO, so the HVO could not hit it with their fire. Then people, women, children, usually came there with canisters and different vessels in order to get some water from the truck and to take it home. I personally was a witness. My young daughter was present when other people were hit.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right, I think we can proceed beyond this now. Apart from the water -- the distribution of water - and I do want to conclude on this part of your testimony, sir - were there any other public gatherings, types of public gatherings during your experience, the months that you were in Mostar during this time, were targeted either for rifle fire, artillery fire, what have you? For instance, just to move us, funerals.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already said that any movement was highly risky. I don't know whether that existed anywhere in the world, this kind of administration that was created so fast on the other side. And the administration imposed a curfew. People were not allowed to move about during the day, in daytime. There were also other gatherings that took place, and that is funerals, when the dead were being buried.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And what would happen at that time?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, because we were the target of attacks, because these deaths occurred every day, we could not conduct funerals at the same time every day. We tried to conceal this from the enemy, and usually this was done during the night with very few people present in order to avoid the risk of someone being killed or injured.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, I want you to go forward, please, and look at the next -- again, I'm going to ask you to look at the next couple of exhibits as a group. If you can direct your attention, please, and familiarise yourself so you know what you're looking at. Exhibit 422, 421, 425 -- excuse me -- 462.1. Can you tell the Chamber, please, are all these letters or correspondence that you were involved in raising various issues and concerns either to the international community or through the international representatives in the area or directly to leaders of the HVO or the Croat side?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What we lived through in Mostar was a catastrophe. We simply wanted the world to know. We wanted to find some compassion, a trace of compassion that would bring goodness to the fore, so that the shelling and killing of people would be condemned, and that is why we protested to the bishop. We asked him to visit us. We asked Cardinal Kuharic to visit us from Croatia, and also Bishop Puljic from Sarajevo. We also asked the international community for protection because this simply went beyond our possibilities of ...

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Smajkic, I'm sorry, but I think we'll have to let, to some extent, the letters to speak for themselves. But let me ask you a couple questions -- or one or two questions about each one.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Exhibit 422, an invitation to leaders of the local Catholic church. My question to you is very simple, and please respond: Did those persons ever, in fact, come to East Mostar and assist you in the way that you requested?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They didn't come. We did not get any answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If you look at Exhibit P421, the next in the bundle, which, for the record, it makes, again, a reference to the killing of Salem Mezit in the first sentence of the text itself, did you receive any satisfactory response from the HVO leadership to this letter dated the 29th of May, 1993?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not get any answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me direct your attention to 425. In this letter, I think just to make --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'll do this as quickly as possible, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In the first paragraph, you were requesting -- this is a letter directed to Mr. Petkovic and Mr. J. Topic. Is that signed by you? It is signed by you, is it not?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Directing your attention, and the courtroom's attention, to the first paragraph, is it accurate to say that this was a letter to some of the Bosnian-Croat leaders to allow some Muslim holidays, Islamic holidays, to be observed with some measure of peace, or at least a cease-fire. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can you tell the Chamber, please, did the HVO, in fact, agree to either a ceasing or lessening of hostile activities at that time, or what happened?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say to you - and you have probably noticed by now, having followed what I said - that we simply tried to take any kind of action in order to reduce fire or to bring about a total cease-fire. Since the great Muslim holiday of Bajram was about to start on the 1st of June, we availed ourselves of that opportunity to send an appeal to the international community, and especially the military forces - that is to say, the military command and also to Mr. Topic, as the representative of the administration - to have at least a temporary cease-fire then so that the believers could spend the Bajram holiday in a dignified manner. We went even further and suggested that those three or four days that we would have for the holidays could, perhaps, help extend the cease-fire beyond those three or four days of holiday. That was our suggestion. However, unfortunately, it was not only that there was no cease-fire, but the fire became even more intensive. That was the response we got.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And finally, for these purposes, on 462.1, this is a letter - and apologising for the quality of the copy of the last portions of the letter - but is this a letter that was sent by you that was, in fact, to be communicated to the Pope through the Spanish Battalion?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was in contact with the Spaniards who were in Medjurgorje. And they said that it was possible for them to convey that letter of mine to that particular address. May I, Your Honours, remind you that at the beginning of 1993, I called on the Pope. I was received by him, together with the bishop, and I was told that I should do -- people were telling me that I should do anything to make this stop. So I remembered that, and I reminded him that I was on a mission -- on a good mission of peace when I went to see him, and I hoped that this appeal would reach him and that it would be of mutual benefit, something to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me just briefly direct your attention to the part on the cover sheet, if you will, the second page of the letter itself, about the middle of that document -- excuse me, that page. And just to move to the next part of your testimony, in addition to the killing of Salem Mezit, were you also bringing to the Pope's attention the mistreatment of other Islamic clerics, as well as civilians, and the destruction of mosques?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In that regard, then, putting the letter aside, moving forward, can you tell the Chamber, during this -- roughly this period of time, this April, May, June 1993 time period, what was -- to your knowledge, what was happening to many of the local Islamic officials, imams, that sort of thing? What was happening to them?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the imams who were reached by the HVO forces were taken prisoner. Those who managed to save themselves in this exodus managed to get away. But all of those who were captured, some were even killed. I know that 12 were taken prisoner. 12 imams were taken prisoner, and they were kept in camps for a month or two, three, nine months, up to a year, as a matter of fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. I can say that these are imams who were in the territory of Herzegovina; that is to say, Capljina, Stolac, Mostar. However, also, the Mufti of the Tuzla region, a high Islamic official, should be added to that. Even before May, in April, he was taken prisoner by the HVO, and he was kept in prison for six months, and he was exchanged for some other persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. I'm going to come back to this in just a moment. Let me go back for a moment to a couple of other documents before we move on. If I can, in the -- next in the bundle, you should have 467.2 and 476.1. And I think I'm just going to simply ask you, 467.2, is that a letter from the Catholic Bishop in Mostar to you, dated the 19th of June, 1993?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And Exhibit 476.1, is that a letter written by you to the Catholic Bishop, dated the 24th of June, 1993, and is that essentially in response to the letter which is 467.2?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm just going to leave those letters to speak for themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, concerning the imams, you said there were approximately at least 12 that you knew to be detained.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I can have the usher's assistance--

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: -- could the witness be shown, and also distributed in the courtroom, please, what's been marked as P882? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Smajkic, is it fair to say -- be transparent about this, in order to present this as efficiently as possible in the courtroom and to avoid the spelling of many names for the record -- I asked you to provide me a list of these 12 imams. And is the list that's now been placed in front of you, P882, a list of those 12 imams that you've been telling us about in the last few minutes?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And the information in the right column, is that -- does that indicate essentially their area of religious responsibility, or where they were located?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Touching on a few more of -- on this same topic, but a person not on this list -- yes, please?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, there is a mistake. Number ten, Asim Smajkic. "K," is -- should be deleted. It's not Smajkic. It's Smajic, without a "K."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, going on, beyond this list of 12 imams who were imprisoned during this time, did -- directing your attention to an imam named Musan Becirevic, can you tell the Chamber what happened to him?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a retired imam who was cruelly and brutally killed in the mosque in which he lived. He is not on this list. He was captured at home, and they did different things with him. They demonstrated all kinds of things on him. They made him kneel, and they killed him in such a way, in the mosque itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me ask you - and I've been a bit delinquent in the last few minutes - when you talked about the 12 imams being imprisoned or detained, who, to your knowledge, were they imprisoned or detained by? Of course, I'm not asking you for individual names, but by what group or organisation were these imams detained or imprisoned?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The armed forces of the HVO, the HVO police.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And concerning the -- Imam Becirevic, who was it that killed him in the mosque -- in his mosque?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were the armed units who at that time, during that offensive, which had started on the 9th of May, had expelled the Muslim peoples. Some were taken to the camps, some were expelled to the other side of the river, and some were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The armed units of what organisation or group?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. They were the HVO armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me mention to you another name - excuse me - and he is number 1 on the list that you provided to us a moment ago. Can you tell us what happened very briefly to Zlomuzica - excuse me for that - number 1 on the list? My apologies.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was a man who, along with several of other people, had fled to the woods when the attack had begun, and even the newspapers in Croatia reported that there was an imam who had fled to the hills and who had some armed unit with him, and who was a threat to that order that was to be built, according to the HVO. So they organised a real posse. They went after him, and they found him in the forest. Then they took him to the camp, and he experienced terrible brutality and torture. All his teeth were knocked out. He has no teeth left now. And this was done with either a handle of either a hoe or a shovel. He was beaten with that handle all over his body. They hung him from -- by the feet, and he was tortured in that position. He still is suffering consequences of this brutal mistreatment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Just one further question on that: You said there were reports in the papers in Croatia that he was somehow involved with an armed unit in the hills. Can you tell us whether or not, to your knowledge, was that true? Was he leading an armed unit in the hills?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He took shelter in the woods with civilians, but propaganda turned him into a commander of an armed unit, and then they went after him to capture him, and they exacted a revenge on him. This was reported in the newspapers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me next turn your attention to another imam named Kasim Mezit. Do you know, in the course of your professional duties as the Mufti of Mostar, one of your imams called Kasim Mezit? Sir?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And is it correct -- so the Chamber will know, is it correct that unfortunately Mr. Mezit died approximately ten months ago?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Have you, through various inquiries of your own, including speaking with his wife, learned what happened to Mr. Mezit, or one of the things that happened to Mr. Mezit, around this time?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They all believe that he died as a result of torture in the camp and of the consequences of what he had gone through during his capture. I personally saw him on a number of times. He had to be under constant medical care. He had a problem with his back. His backbone was injured, and he had to go to rehabilitation, and he often complained about his ailments.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Smajkic, what I'm going to ask you about, I should have also asked you. You mentioned his wife. And were you in fact also, as you've just told us now, in close communication with Mr. Mezit while he was still alive?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, please listen to my question and answer this question: Did Mr. Mezit tell you anything that happened to him around the 7th of May, approximately, 1993?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Tell the Chamber, please, what Mr. Mezit told you happened to him.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Mezit was captured by the HVO in the middle of the street before the 9th of May; that is, before the offensive against Mostar and against the civilians. We did not know where he was taken. Later on, we learned that he was in a camp and he spent several months there. I cannot say exactly. However, when he came back, he told about terrible torture that he was subjected to, both in the camp and, in particular, during the investigation that was conducted against him by Mr. Tuta in person.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, before we continue on - probably everyone in the courtroom realises this - but this is the Kasim Mezit that is listed as number 12 on the list that you gave us a few minutes ago?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, please, tell us what happened to Mr. Mezit when he told you about the -- his dealings, his contact with Tuta.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He told me that his interrogation was conducted personally by Mr. Tuta himself. He said that he was given a piece of paper to write down certain information which Mr. Tuta needed about the state of affairs in the army, which he needed, about his participation or membership in there and some other things.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me stop for one moment. Do you know where this interrogation took place? Did he tell you that?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He told me that he was brought there in a car; I'm not exactly sure from which prison. I don't know whether he was in Listica or Ljubuski; one of these places. But he was brought to the Heliodrom -- I think it was actually Listica, because Mr. Jahic was also there and that was mentioned, and he said that at that time that he had seen Mr. Jahic there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me stop you for a moment because I'm not sure the Chamber had heard about this before now. Is Listica another name, a prior name, for a town called Siroki Brijeg?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: When was the name of that town - if you know, approximately - when was the name of that town changed from Listica to Siroki Brijeg?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was changed in 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can you tell the Chamber, please, between those two names, Listica and Siroki Brijeg, is one of those a Muslim name and one of them a Croat name for the same town?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There's no distinction there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you know why the name was changed to Siroki Brijeg?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would take some time to explain it, but that used to be a name before. But then during the communist era, that name was changed. I don't think that there's much importance in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: At this point in time, we won't pursue it further. But the point is, this is the same place also called Siroki Brijeg; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Right. Continue on, then. This interrogation that took place of Kasim Mezit at Siroki Brijeg, what happened? You said he was given a paper by Tuta and told to write things down. What happened after that?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, to write it down. As he did not know what to write down in order to satisfy Mr. Tuta, he wrote down a few lines. But he took the paper and crumpled it and threw it away and said to start again.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Who took the paper --

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This went on for several times. Tuta did, who took the paper and threw it away, because he was not happy with what was -- what had been written down.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And what happened next?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Next, he threatened him, and he told him if he didn't write down what he was asked to do, that he would gouge his eyes out.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And did anything else happen to Mr. Mezit around that time?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Mezit started writing again and didn't have anything to write. And when he didn't receive the information that he wanted - this is what Mr. Mezit told me at that time - Mr. Tuta took the pencil from his hand and stuck it in his face, and he broke it against his jaw.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Who stuck the pencil in whose face?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Tuta stuck it in Mr. Mezit's face.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Moving on, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: We are turning, Mr. President, to the final topic of the direct examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Smajkic, I would like to turn your attention now specifically to the question of the destruction of cultural and religious properties. And could you introduce this topic, please. Can you tell the Chamber generally what you observed about the HVO or HDZ conduct toward signs and symbols of Bosniak society.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Anything that was evocative in terms of architecture - not only the religious structures, but there is an oriental influence in Mostar in residential architecture, including the old bridge, which is a symbol of the city, and a number of mosques and other infrastructure - all that was targeted by the artillery and by other weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you look next at Exhibit 739.1. Can you just describe what that document is to the Chamber and what that's about, what it indicates.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a document about the destruction and damage sustained by the Islamic structure in my area.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Smajkic, I think you've jumped one too far. Forgive me. If you go to 739.1 -- it's a very short exhibit, before you get to the one I think you're referring to now. If you go back, please.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't orient myself. I don't know what you are referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The document you are looking at is -- I believe you're looking at P868 which, of course, is the next document we will get to. But there should be P739.1 before then, unless there's been -- it's quite possible there has been an error.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Does the Chamber have 739.1? Yes, that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That's it. That's it. Thank you very much. Take a moment, please, to look at that so you know what it is. And then can you just tell the Chamber what that document is about and what it indicates.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that we need to spend any time on this document. It is very clear to me. This is all the streets in Mostar whose names have been changed after the expulsion of Muslims; that is, some streets were changed even while we were there, without any consultation of the Muslim partners. They got new names so that the person who goes back to Mostar now, after seven or eight years, and who was born in Mostar, if he is to go there now, he could not orient himself there at all. What is characteristic about these names is that they are 100 per cent historical figures, religious leaders, a number of friars and writers and so on, of Croatian people. This just speaks to the fact that this whole area was attempted to be turned into a Croatian area.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Two follow-up questions to finish, Mr. President, if I'm allowed, so we can finish with this document before the pause.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Very specifically, Mr. Smajkic - and please, short answers, if you can - who changed the names of these streets?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Croatian -- the Croat authority, the Croatian Defence Council. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The names on the right side in the column, the new names, if you will, you were telling us -- just a moment ago, you said --

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You said these were --

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Take number --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me ask you a general question -- or not general, but perhaps different than the one you're about to mention. You said a moment ago these were 100 per cent historical figures, religious leaders, a number of friars, et cetera, and these were all of what national or ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Of what national --

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Croat ethnic group.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. All right. With the President's indulgence, you said, I think, you wanted to point out one particular name as an example. Can you do that briefly, please?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Number 1, Square Rondo, is the square of Croatian --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What's the new name? Just tell us briefly, what is the new name, if you can tell us that, in Croatian?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The new name is Nikola Subic Zrinski. For instance, under 9, street of Safeta Mujica.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I hoped we could do this very quickly before the break, but it may take another minute or two. If we could take the pause now. And I can tell the Chamber I had sincerely hoped to finish this witness before the first break but have not quite made it, but I would hope to be finished shortly after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, we will adjourn until 11.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott. Please continue with your direct examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Smajkic, I want to conclude on this exhibit, 739.1. We didn't have really quite time to finish with clarity comments that you were making before the break. At one point, I think you referred to number 1, but then when you took us across the page, you took us to number 2. So if we can start fresh on that point. You seem to want to indicate to us, give us some examples of some of the name changes from those in the left-hand column to those in the right-hand column. So would you just tell us -- obviously we're not going to go through anything like the entire list, but perhaps you can give us one or two examples.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I shall give the example under number 9, Safet Mujic. He was a well-known doctor, a Bosniak, and his street was renamed the street of Prince Domagoj. You have registered that, haven't you? Then number 13, Maha Djikic. It was renamed into the street of King Tomislav. Then street under number 26, Mostaric. It was renamed Dr. Barisa Smoljan. Then 41, the street of Mujo Bjelavac. That was a Muslim name. And then it was renamed the street of Father Ambro Miletic, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me go back for a moment, if I followed you correctly. In terms of the --

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Liska.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In terms of the name in the right column for item number 26 that you gave us, can you tell us what you know about that person. I'm not sure that name necessarily means much to us. But Dr. Smoljan, who was that person, if you know?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Muslim person, Mostaric. It was due to his merits that the street was named after him. But then the street was renamed Dr. Barisa Smoljan.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And I asked you who is Dr. Smoljen?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Smoljan is some Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I am finished that with exhibit. Concerning the mosques in Mostar, both the east and the west side, if you can say, can you tell the Chamber, please, briefly, the state of those mosques by the end of the fighting with the HVO in approximately February or March, 1994? What was the condition or state of the mosques in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of them were totally destroyed. We can say that some mosques were not totally destroyed. Their roofs were damaged, their walls, but I can say to you that out of the 20 mosques in town, there was not a single one that could receive believers who were supposed to come for prayers. It was large-scale destruction, those who were razed to the ground, to those who were considerably, considerably damaged - 80 per cent, for instance - and they could therefore not be used for their original purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, I want you to tell the Chamber, please, if you can -- and then I'm going to ask you the basis for whatever it is your answer is. Can you tell the Chamber, based on what you saw during those months in Mostar -- can you make any observations about whether the mosques were damaged by what we might call collateral damage or accidental fire or whether, in your view, they were deliberately targeted? And whatever your view is, please tell the Chamber why.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were selected targets, quite precisely selected, targeted and fired at with the aim of being destroyed. This list of names, street names that we just saw, shows quite clearly that not a single name -- not a single street was any longer named by a prominent Muslim. There was not a single street in town that was still named after a prominent Muslim. Everybody knew that from the very inception of the Croat Community of Herceg-Bosna, the town of Mostar was proclaimed the capital of the Croats. In the heads of the people who had charted such policies, it seemed inconceivable --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Seric?

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Your Honour, for this line of testimony. The witness is here to testify and not to prosecute or to think of what others may have thought.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Witness, I think the question is quite simple, only concerning the mosques rather than those streets.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Smajkic, you expressed -- let me rephrase. Let me focus you, please. Forgive me for a moment, please. The question I put to you was for you to express your observation of what you believe happened to the mosques. And I asked you, and my question to you is - you must tell the Chamber, of course, on what you base that - but why do you say, in your view, that they were deliberately targeted? Now, please confine your answer specifically to that.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I started to, but then you wouldn't let me. I didn't want to talk about the streets. I wanted to say just one more sentence, and then I would have been quite clear. The Croat Defence Council, or rather, the Croat Republic of Herceg-Bosna, proclaimed Mostar a Croat town. How can it be a Croat town if there were 20 mosques and 20 minarets there? They have to be destroyed, razed to the ground, so that it could be turned into a so-called Croat town. That is quite clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: As the senior Islamic church official for the region of Herzegovina and for the mosques in particular in Mostar, can you tell the Chamber please, as far as you know, were any of the mosques used by the ABiH or Bosniak forces for military purposes?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never, never, not in a single case.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm going to direct your attention to Exhibit 868.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And it will be the final document, Mr. President, in everyone's bundle of documents. It's a bit thick, but of course, two-thirds of it is the other translations, both in French -- well, the original B/C/S version, the French version, and the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell the Chamber what this is, Exhibit P868?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a report, review of mosques destroyed or damaged in the territory that I covered.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What role did you play in the preparation of this report?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I played a key role. By your leave, I have to note that there was a mistake, just one. I noticed it only later. It concerns the mosque in Livno -- or the mosques in Livno. You can find that -- I do apologise for this mistake, this error. It has to be corrected. Let me just take a look, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: To assist the courtroom, I think he is referring to --

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Livno.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I think that was roman numeral section V.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What would you like to correct, please?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The mosque in Grborez under number 3 was not destroyed. It was not destroyed. But recently -- or rather, even two or three days after Dayton, hand grenades were thrown several times because Bosniak people started coming back to that area and it has been seriously damaged.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Let's not pursue that further at this time. All right. Is it accurate that - as you told us yesterday - that all these facilities, whether it's a mosque -- I'm not sure there's other religious buildings that are included in your report. These are all religious facilities that were under essentially your responsibility; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, I would like to direct your attention --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, let me, Mr. President -- I'm not going to go through this document at length. Obviously the Chamber has it, or will have it if it's admitted, and can review it at length.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let's just see how this works. The first section under roman numeral I(a), although I see there actually seems to be two I(a)'s. But in the middle of the first page, it says: "Mostar Stari Grad, Old Town." And then what you've done is list the demolished mosques in that section. And then it goes from demolished mosques on to the next section of damaged mosques. Is that the way, basically, that the report works, sir?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Directing your attention -- and I'm going to try to do this by reference numbers, because the pages in the various versions might not be the same. But if you can turn to -- if you can find the section for the Southwest Mostar municipality. And I'm afraid the numbering, at least in mine, is a bit hard to follow because there's a series of number 1s and subheadings. But doesn't matter. If you can please find the section titled "Southwest Mostar Municipality." Do you have that? Do you have it?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know it all by heart.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Well, it may assist if we refer to it by section so other people in the courtroom can also follow. Under "Demolished Mosque" in that section, number 1, can you just simply confirm for us when you refer there to the Dervis Pasa mosque, is that the mosque that you identified this morning as one of the mosques destroyed on the 9th or 10th of May, 1993?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was subjected to attacks all the time. Only its ruins are still there; that is to say, a few badly damaged walls and nothing else, totally damaged. This mosque was not razed to the ground, but it was destroyed totally.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. In your report, you say, reading the next sentence: "The area of the city in which this mosque was situated was under the control of Vinko Martinovic, Stela." What was that based on? Can you tell us what information was used to make that statement in the report?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wrote that because everybody knows, and all the people who came from the west side knew, that this was the zone where Mr. Stela operated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Seric.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, although we have heard both the question and the answer, since there is a problem with reviewing the text, please disregard both the question and the answer, because the Prosecutor has already omitted such acts from the indictment. In the amended indictment, these acts are no longer there. They were omitted by the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Scott, could you give us an explanation on this very point.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour. It's not being offered for the purposes -- counsel is absolutely right, in terms of the charge. It's not being offered to suggest, at least for purposes of the charges in the indictment, that Mr. Martinovic was responsible for the destruction of that mosque. But it does tend to identify, further confirm that part of Mostar which was under his control. It's offered for that purpose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, you may proceed, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I might also indicate that he is charged, in fact, with persecution in count 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Would you please, then, go to item 3 under that same heading. You Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. mentioned a mosque in the settlement of Balinovac.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, I'm not going to read that out loud, because everyone in the courtroom will have that, but I'm going to ask you a similar question: On what basis do you indicate that soldiers commanded by Tuta were involved in the mosque -- this mosque being destroyed?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was noticed by people who were being taken away by the HVO forces right by the mosque itself, because that was the road that led to the west and to the camps and other prisons. So these people noticed the exact day, the 9th, when the offensive was launched. That's when it was destroyed, and even the foundations could no longer be seen.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. I'm going to direct your attention now to roman numeral III, which is titled, "Religious Council of the Islamic Community of Jablanica." You indicate there under "Demolished Mosques," number 1, the mosque in the settlement of Sovici, destroyed by explosives after the Bosniaks had been expelled from the settlement. Number 2, the mosque in the settlement of Doljani, it was set on fire and destroyed after the massacre of the inhabitants of the village. There are indications that the units that did it were under the command of Naletilic, Tuta. And I ask you again, what was the basis for these observations, first starting, if you will, with the destruction of the mosque in Sovici, if you can give us that answer first, and then if you can turn your attention to Doljani, please.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are two villages and two neighbouring mosques. The two villages are adjacent. After the massacre that was committed against the population of Sovici and Doljani, under number 1 and 2, part of the civilians were expelled to Jablanica, the municipal centre of Jablanica. Refugees, ex-police, at that particular place that I visited, told me that this was done by the units under Tuta.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Did you have occasion, as part of this work, or people acting under your direction, to interview refugees and persons in Jablanica about these matters?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. We have a department of the Islamic community in Jablanica, and they are more familiar with these problems than I am, but this was said to us in my presence and in the presence of the imam from Jablanica during my visit there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And with the one correction that you've made, sir, this morning - for which we thank you - concerning the mosque in Livno, do you believe, to the best of your knowledge, that this report, which is P868, is accurate?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Smajkic, I have no further questions for you. I apologise if I sometimes interrupted you. I did not mean any disrespect, but I was trying to move the taking of the testimony along a bit. I thank you very much. Mr. President I have no questions -- further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Cross-examinations? Mr. Krsnik? I have to remind you that when you are cross-examining the witness, please be polite and do fairness to the witness. And another thing is that if you want to show some documents to this witness, as a rule of this Chamber, you have to distribute it before your cross-examination rather than lead us from one document to another. You may proceed, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. By all means, I shall abide by your instructions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, witness.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I am Defence counsel for the accused Mladen Naletilic, so I'm going to put some questions to you. I shall always try to phrase my questions in such a way in order to get concise and short answers. We both speak the same language, so could we please both of us pause so that the interpreters can interpret this into the official languages of the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please be so kind as to answer my first question: Why do you claim that the Croat Community of Herceg-Bosna is an illegal organisation?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because it did not recognise or doesn't recognise the constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the laws stemming from the constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: You know that the HZ HB was precisely established on the basis of the constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina, because that is what the constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina allows to every one of the constituent peoples, and you know that the HZ HB is an organisation within Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that you also know --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm going to have to object to that as a factual inaccuracy, the characterisation of putting that question to the witness because, as Mr. Krsnik knows, the constitutional court of Bosnia-Herzegovina declared Herceg-Bosna to be unconstitutional and illegal.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You may rephrase your question, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, by your leave, may I give an explanation? The constitutional court of Bosnia-Herzegovina passed that decision in 1993, in different political and historic circumstances, and we are going to get to that during the cross-examination. But now I'm talking about 1992, and because of some of the questions that were put by my learned friend, I will have to put one question related to 1991. Therefore, Your Honours, when speaking of 1992, there is no recognition of the independent state of Bosnia-Herzegovina, there is no ruling of the constitutional court, and my questions will lead to that. And I don't know whether this present witness is testifying here as a politician, as a religious authority, or as an individual, as a person, in his private capacity.
